We looked at the restaurants within a mile of 910 U.S. college campuses.

The most common kind of restaurant near campus? Pizza. It's the top type near 38% of those campuses, and one of the top three near 71%.
Mexican food is the most common type near 22% of campuses. After that: sandwich shops (8%), American restaurants (7%) and coffee shops (6%).

A typical campus in our data has about 50 places to eat within a mile, and about 15 within half a mile.

And 71% of all the restaurants we counted are local places, not chains.
What's the most common food near your campus? Every campus, closest places first: https://www.savorscout.net/campus/

Eating alone at a restaurant feels awkward for one reason: you're in the wrong seat.

A table for two in the middle of a room full of couples feels exposed. A counter doesn't.

At a counter or a bar, eating alone is the normal thing to do. Ramen counters, sushi counters, diner counters, taco counters.

You get served faster, you can leave whenever you want, and you get to watch someone cook.

What makes a place good for eating alone:

• A counter or bar that serves the full menu
• An open kitchen
• One-person dishes: ramen, a rice bowl, pasta, a sandwich
• Somewhere busy, where nobody notices how long you stay

And the best part: it's the one meal where you order exactly what you want, with no negotiating.

More: https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/eating-alone
Pizza is the most common restaurant near U.S. college campuses. Here's how to tell a good pizza place from the rest, before you order:

1. Look at the edge of the crust.

Dark, uneven blisters on the rim mean a very hot oven and well-fermented dough. A pale crust that's the same color all over usually means a conveyor oven.

2. Count the toppings.

Good pizzerias put about three things on a pie, not nine. Too many toppings release water and steam the crust soggy.

3. Taste the sauce.

It should taste like tomatoes: simple and bright. A thick, sweet sauce is usually covering for tomatoes that weren't worth tasting.

4. Lift a slice.

A little oil on top is fine. A puddle of grease underneath means too much cheap cheese and a crust that wasn't baked hot enough.

More: https://www.savorscout.net/food/pizza

"Open until 2am" is a plan, not a promise. Plenty of kitchens stop cooking hours before the listing says they close.

How to actually find food after 11pm:

1. Read the reviews, not the hours.

A recent review that says "went at 1am, kitchen still open" is worth more than any hours listing.

2. An open bar doesn't mean an open kitchen.

The closing time you see is usually the bar's. The kitchen can close well before it, so a busy bar isn't proof you can get food.

3. Go to places built for late night: 24-hour diners, taquerias near nightlife, Korean and Chinese kitchens that stay open late, halal carts.

A kitchen that does most of its business after midnight is good after midnight.

4. Call before you walk over. Thirty seconds on the phone beats a 20-minute walk to a locked door.

And skip delivery after midnight: the kitchen can be open with no driver willing to bring it.

More: https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/late-night
